question: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Hildegard Bentele (PPE), Rihards Kols (ECR), Tomáš Kubín (PfE), Alice Teodorescu Måwe (PPE), Antonio López-Istúriz White (PPE) Subject:

On 4 May 2026, a Ramallah Court1 ordered the Palestinian Authority (PA) to resume payments under the ‘pay-for-slay’ scheme – officially known as the Martyrs Fund – to the family of a man held in an Israeli prison. This ruling and reports by Reuters2 and The Jerusalem Post3 raise serious questions as to whether the pay-for-slay scheme has been or will be truly abolished as President Abbas claimed during a Fatah conference, when he said that the PA had restructured its payments to no longer reflect the prisoner’s sentences but to distribute the funds in the form of social welfare. Commissioner Šuica explained in an answer to earlier questions that these social welfare allowances are now based on vulnerability criteria4, as requested by the EU5. 1.

How does the Commission respond to this court ruling and the criticism that the PA reforms only amount to cosmetic restructuring designed to satisfy Western donors while preserving the pay-for-slay-scheme domestically?

Since the Commission emphasised ‘democratic, transparent and efficient governance’ as a condition for EU funding, what benchmarks has the PA actually met so far and can the Commission publish the agreed Reform Matrix and milestones?
Can the Commission confirm that no EU funds are used or will be used to support prisoners, terrorists and/or their families?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026) On 10 February 2025, by Presidential decree 4/20251, the Palestinian Authority (PA) abolished the previous prisoners and martyrs’ payment system and established a new social system based exclusively on socio-economic and vulnerability criteria. An independent and international audit contracted by the PA of the new system is ongoing since January 2026. The EU has also launched its own comprehensive system audit to verify that no parallel payment system is in place. This audit is expected to be completed by the end of 2026. The May 2026 court ruling reported by the Times of Israel concerns an individual case arising from the application of the previous legal framework governing prisoners' entitlements. It does not call into question the overall reform currently being implemented. Most funds disbursed by the EU to the PA are linked to its progress on reforms in the areas of fiscal sustainability, including social protection, good governance, private sector development and the provision of public services. The Reform Matrix is a working document attached to the Financing Agreements with the PA of 2025 and 2026-2027, which is not for public dissemination. The Commission has always excluded financial support to the prisoners and martyrs’ payment system. Part of the EU’s funding contributes to the PA’s social allowances to vulnerable individuals and families, allocated on the basis of socio-economic criteria. All financial support is subject to robust controls and safeguards to ensure that EU funds are used only for their intended purposes. The EU applies a strict vetting process to the beneficiaries of its payments and tracks each financial transfer to vetted individuals.
